question: Why do 23 people give even odds of a shared birthday?

scene.title: Why do 23 people give even odds of a shared birthday?
scene.subtitle: In a room of just 23 people, at least two share a birthday about half the time. Most people guess you would need far more.
scene.why: Coincidences in a group are more common than they feel, because every pair is a chance for a match, not just pairs that include you.
scene.opening: How many people must be in a room before two of them probably share a birthday? Most people guess far more than 23.

beats.title: Just you: 22 chances
beats.body: In a room of 23 people, the chance that someone shares your birthday is only about 6%. You are in just 22 pairs, one with each other person, and each pair is a 1 in 365 chance.

beats.title: Anyone with anyone: 253 chances
beats.body: But a match can be between any two people. 23 people make 253 pairs, each a 1 in 365 chance. About 253 such chances give even odds: a match half the time.

beats.title: One arrival at a time
beats.body: Now let people arrive one by one. Each newcomer has more birthdays to hit, so a match gets likelier with every arrival. After the 23rd, the chance that nobody matches has fallen to just under half, so the chance of a match is just over half.

beats.title: Why 50 is almost certain
beats.body: Pairs grow far faster than people: 50 people make 1,225 pairs, almost five times as many as 23 people make. With 50 in the room, a shared birthday is 97% likely.

scene.takeaway: A match can be between any two people, so 23 people make 253 chances, not 22. That is enough for about even odds that two share a birthday.

questions.q: How many other people would you need before someone probably shares your own birthday?
questions.a: About 253, since that many 1 in 365 chances give even odds; 23 people happen to make exactly 253 pairs. Even 180 others would give you only a 39% chance.

questions.q: Do 253 pairs mean a 253 in 365 chance, about 69%?
questions.a: No. 253 divided by 365 is how many matching pairs to expect on average, about 0.7. Some rooms have two or three matches, and about half have none, so the chance of at least one is 51%.

questions.q: Real birthdays bunch up in some months. Does that make a match more or less likely?
questions.a: Slightly more likely: when some dates are more common, two people land on the same one a little more often. 23 people still give just over even odds.
